Edwards Amasa Park
ed'wərdz ə-mā'sə pärk
n. (Edwards Amasa Park, 1808–1900, Andover professor, last systematizer of the New England theology)
English surname Park, from a dweller by an enclosed ground; named for Jonathan Edwards.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Edwards Amasa Park taught at Andover Theological Seminary for more than fifty years and was the last and ablest defender of the New England theology as a distinct tradition descending from Jonathan Edwards through Edwards the younger, Smalley, Emmons, and Taylor. His 1850 address, The Theology of the Intellect and That of the Feelings, distinguished the language of doctrine stated for the understanding from the language of piety addressed to the affections, and argued that much apparent disagreement between orthodox parties is a confusion of the two registers. Charles Hodge answered him at length in the Princeton Review, holding that the distinction, however useful pastorally, becomes a device for holding two inconsistent doctrines at once. Park also edited the collected works of Emmons and wrote the standard memoirs of the school. Isa 8:20 is the test Hodge applied and the dictionary applies with him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines intellect as the faculty of the human soul which receives and compares ideas, and feeling as the sense of touch, or an emotion of the mind.

expand to see more

IN'TELLECT, n. That faculty of the human soul or mind, which receives or comprehends the ideas communicated to it by the senses or by perception, or other means.

FEEL'ING, n. The sense of touch; the sensation produced by the touch; also, an emotion or passion of the mind.

DOC'TRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; whatever is laid down as true by an instructor or master.

Key Scripture

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

1Co 2:14 — "But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

Eph 4:14 — "That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;"

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Modern Corruption

He distinguished the theology of the intellect from that of the feelings, and the distinction became a hiding place.

expand to see more

Park's distinction has a real use. Scripture does speak of God in the language of affection and of relenting, and a dogmatician who flattens every such passage into a proposition will misread the Psalms. But Hodge saw the danger and named it: once the two registers are separated in principle, a man may preach what he does not hold and hold what he does not preach, and the doctrinal statement ceases to govern the pulpit. Tit 1:9 requires the elder to hold fast the faithful word so that he may “exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — one word, serving both purposes.

The dictionary's judgment is that Park's scheme functioned as the last refuge of a tradition that had already surrendered imputation and inability and wished to keep the Edwardsean name. Eph 4:14 describes the result of such flexibility: men “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14). Andover's subsequent history, in which the seminary moved to the progressive theology of the 1880s within a generation of Park's retirement, is the evidence. A distinction that cannot be cashed out in propositions will not hold a seminary.

Usage

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the test Hodge applied."

"“carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — where the distinction led."

"“to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — one word for both registers."
